findings.summary: Bootstrapping is a statistical procedure that estimates the distribution of an estimator by resampling original data with replacement. It generates many simulated samples from the observed dataset, calculates a statistic for each, and uses the resulting histogram to approximate sampling variability, standard errors, and confidence intervals without relying on parametric assumptions. Its accuracy improves with larger numbers of resamples, though 50 to 100 samples often suffice for standard error estimation.

mechanisms.title: Resampling with replacement
mechanisms.explanation: The original observed data set is repeatedly sampled, each time drawing units independently with replacement to form a 'bootstrap sample' of the same size. This creates many slightly different samples, reflecting the uncertainty of the original draw.

mechanisms.title: Statistic calculation on resamples
mechanisms.explanation: For each bootstrap sample, the chosen estimator (e.g., mean, correlation) is computed. The collection of these bootstrap estimates forms an empirical distribution that approximates the sampling distribution of the statistic.

unknowns: Finite-sample performance guarantees beyond asymptotic consistency
Optimal number of resamples for specific statistics and sample sizes
Behavior under dependent or non-i.i.d. data structures
Automation limitations in traditional statistical software packages
